name: Pick up LTL freight from shippers
summary: A city driver collects a shipper's pallets and brings them back to the origin terminal for the evening dock. At the shipper the driver checks in, waits for the freight and a door, checks the bill of lading and any dangerous goods paperwork, counts and inspects the pieces, loads and secures them, labels them with PRO numbers and scans the bill on the handheld. Freight not ready, busy docks, missing paperwork and sites without a dock are the usual delays, and the freight then rides on the truck until the driver returns to the terminal at the end of the route.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with 540 city drivers on weekday day shifts, handhelds for pickup scans and bill images.
baseline.notes: About 100,000 pickup stops a month carrying about 150,000 shipments (1.5 shipments per stop).

trigger: The driver receives a pickup on the morning manifest or from dispatch during the route.
end_state: The freight is at a strip door of the origin terminal and the bill is with billing, or the pickup is recorded as attempted for rebooking.

volume.seasonality: Autumn peak from September to mid-December; Mondays and Fridays heaviest; pickups cluster between noon and 5 p.m.

evidence.note: Organisation file process map entry.

surge.cause: Autumn shipping peak (September to mid-December retail and industrial restocking)

evidence.note: LTL volumes in Canada rise from September to early December; author's estimate of size.
540 city drivers split their stop time between pickups and deliveries; about 45% of driver time is on pickups. Author's estimate.
Clerks match paper bills to pickups at driver check-in; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process. Author's estimate.

systems.name: Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Document imaging for bills of lading and delivery receipts
Customer web portal (pickup requests, tracing, documents)
Electronic logging devices and telematics platform
Email, phone system and contact centre software

resources.name: Pickup and delivery truck (day-cab tractor or straight truck)

steps.name: Receive the pickup on the handheld
steps.description: The city driver gets the pickup as part of the morning manifest or as a message from dispatch during the route, and reads the address, ready and closing times, pieces, weight and notes such as liftgate or dangerous goods.

evidence.note: Pickups are relayed to drivers during the route; advanced carriers use handhelds. Time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Drive to the shipper
steps.description: The driver finishes the stops ahead of this one and drives to the shipper, usually after the route's deliveries are done. The wait before is the time the pickup sits behind other stops on the route.

evidence.note: Deliveries are normally run first and pickups follow, with backtracking; urban routes run 50-60 miles and metro routes 90-100 miles a day for up to 20 or more stops. Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Check in at the shipping office
steps.description: The driver parks, goes to the shipping office or window, gives the carrier name and pickup number, and asks which door to use and whether the freight is ready.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Shipper stages the freight and frees a door
steps.description: Shipping staff finish wrapping and labelling the pallets, print the bill of lading and free a dock door. About one pickup in eight finds the freight not ready at all.

evidence.note: Canadian LTL tariffs give 15 minutes free time for shipments up to 500 lb and 30 minutes up to 9,999 lb before waiting time is charged, so waits of this size are ordinary. The not-ready share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide whether to wait or leave
steps.description: The driver asks how long the freight will be and calls the dispatcher, who weighs the other stops and the driver's hours. The driver either waits or leaves and the pickup is rebooked.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Position the truck at the door or curb
steps.description: The driver backs the trailer into the assigned door and sets the brakes, or parks at the curb for a liftgate pickup where there is no dock. Busy shippers make drivers wait for a door.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Receive and check the bill of lading
steps.description: The driver takes the shipper's bill of lading and checks the consignee name and address, number of pieces, weight, description, dangerous goods entries, declared value and special services against the pickup. Missing consignee details, an unreadable bill or a wrong bill-to are the usual problems.

error.defect_description: Wrong consignee, pieces or weight accepted on the bill.

evidence.note: Declared value must be shown on the bill of lading and changes to a bill need written authorisation (Tariff 101 rules 7 and 37). Problem share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Shipper corrects or reprints the bill
steps.description: The shipping clerk fixes the bill of lading or prints a new one; for small shippers without their own form the driver fills in the carrier's blank bill with them.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Check for dangerous goods
steps.description: The driver looks for dangerous goods entries on the bill of lading and for hazard class labels or placards on the pieces before accepting them.

evidence.note: About 5% of LTL shipments carry dangerous goods; author's estimate.

steps.name: Verify the dangerous goods shipping document
steps.description: The driver, who holds a TDG training certificate, checks that the shipping document shows the UN number, shipping name, class, packing group, quantity, 24-hour number and the consignor's certification, that pieces are labelled, and that placards come with the freight when needed. An improperly documented shipment is refused.

control.basis: Transportation of Dangerous Goods Regulations: Part 3 shipping document and Part 6 training certificate

evidence.note: Consignor completes the shipping document before the carrier takes possession and a carrier may refuse an improperly completed one; handlers must hold a training certificate. Refusal share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Count and inspect the pieces
steps.description: The driver counts pallets and loose pieces against the bill, checks wrapping and labels, and looks for damage. About one pickup in fifteen shows a short count, an overage or visible damage.

error.defect_description: Short count or damage missed at pickup and found later at the dock.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Note the exception on the bill and photograph it
steps.description: The driver writes the actual count or the damage on both copies of the bill, has the shipper initial it or mark it shipper load and count, and photographs the freight on the handheld so the claim history starts at pickup.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Choose the loading method
steps.description: Freight at a dock is loaded across the dock plate; freight at a site with no dock comes off the shipper's floor by liftgate and pallet jack.

next.condition: no dock: liftgate or hand load

evidence.note: A site without a dock needs a liftgate. The 18% share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Load the freight at the dock
steps.description: The shipper's forklift operator or the driver with a pallet jack moves the pallets into the trailer; the driver places them in the nose or behind earlier pickups so freight bound for the same terminal stays together and heavy pieces sit on the floor.

evidence.note: The carrier supplies only the driver, and the consignor loads large or heavy articles (Tariff 101 rule 23). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Load the freight by liftgate
steps.description: The driver lowers the liftgate, pulls each pallet onto it with a pallet jack, raises it and pushes the pallet into place, one lift at a time up to the gate's limit.

control.basis: Company liftgate procedure and provincial occupational health and safety rules for material handling

evidence.note: Tailgate service is limited to 1,500 lb per lift (Tariff 101 rule 35). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Secure the load
steps.description: The driver sets load bars or straps behind the freight, or against the previous pickup, so nothing shifts or falls when the truck brakes during the rest of the route.

control.basis: NSC Standard 10 cargo securement as adopted by provincial regulation

evidence.note: Cargo must be contained, immobilised or secured so it cannot shift (NSC Standard 10; Alberta AR 121/2009 s.17(4)).

steps.name: Sign the bill and label the pieces
steps.description: The driver signs the bill of lading, sticks the pre-printed PRO number labels on each handling unit and on the bill, writes the piece count and time, and leaves the shipper's copy.

error.defect_description: PRO label missing from a piece or put on the wrong shipment.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Scan the labels and photograph the bill
steps.description: The driver scans the PRO labels and takes a picture of the bill of lading on the handheld, enters pieces and weight, and closes the stop.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Post the pickup to the TMS
steps.description: The handheld sends the pickup completion, pieces and bill image to the TMS and the imaging system; the shipment's status shows as picked up on the customer portal, and the bill joins the billing entry queue.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Carry the freight to the terminal
steps.description: The freight rides on the truck while the driver makes the remaining stops, then the driver drives back to the terminal at the end of the route. Touch time is this pickup's share of the return drive.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: pickups are made from late morning to about 5 p.m. and drivers return about 4 to 7 p.m.

steps.name: Back into a strip door and hand over
steps.description: The driver backs into the strip door the dock supervisor assigned, or drops the trailer in the yard when no door is free, and tells the dock which pickups are heavy, damaged or dangerous goods.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Match the paper bills to closed pickups
steps.description: The terminal service clerk takes the driver's paper bills, checks each against a closed pickup in the TMS, chases bills that were not imaged or have no matching pickup, and sends the batch to billing for freight bill entry.

error.defect_description: Bill not sent to billing, leaving the shipment unbilled until found.

control.basis: Revenue control: every picked-up shipment has a bill of lading in billing

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Record the attempted pickup
steps.description: The driver records the attempt with a reason code (freight not ready, shipper closed, documents refused) and a photo where useful; the dispatcher rebooks the pickup and the shipper may be billed an attempted-pickup charge.

evidence.note: Attempted pickup charge of $4.25/cwt, minimum $45 (Tariff 101 rule 15).

exceptions.name: Freight not ready
exceptions.description: The shipper has not finished staging or printing the bill; the driver waits or leaves and the pickup is rebooked (about 5% of pickups end as attempts).

exceptions.name: Bill of lading missing or incomplete
exceptions.description: The driver waits while the shipper fixes or reprints the bill or fills in the carrier's form.

exceptions.name: Short, over or damaged at pickup
exceptions.description: The driver notes the exception on the bill and photographs it.

exceptions.name: Dangerous goods without proper documents
exceptions.description: The driver refuses a DG shipment with an incomplete shipping document or missing labels.

exceptions.name: No dock at the site
exceptions.description: The driver loads by liftgate and pallet jack, which takes longer.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from pickup assigned to freight at the terminal door

evidence.note: Author's estimate: advance and standing pickups are on the 7 a.m. manifest but made in the afternoon after deliveries (8 to 10 hours to the terminal door); pickups called in during the day are made within 1 to 3 hours; freight reaches the terminal between 4 and 7 p.m. and the bill is matched at check-in. The mix gives a median near 7 hours.

benchmarks.unit: minutes including driving to the stop

evidence.note: The source uses a 30-minute stop (driving plus time at the stop) as its cost example.

benchmarks.unit: minutes before waiting time is charged, shipments up to 9,999 lb

evidence.note: Tariff 101 rule 38.
US carrier; the organisation file assumes about 2,000 lb for Canadian LTL.

pain_points.description: Drivers wait at shippers for freight to be staged and for a door, and the waiting time is rarely billed.

evidence.note: Tariffs set free time and waiting charges, showing the delay is common; how often it is billed is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Bills of lading arrive incomplete or handwritten and the driver has to check and fix them at the dock, and paper copies must still be matched and sent to billing.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

pain_points.description: Attempted pickups waste a stop and push the pickup to another day.

evidence.note: Attempted pickup charge exists in Canadian tariffs.

pain_points.description: Liftgate pickups at sites without docks take two or three times as long as dock pickups.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Canadian LTL carriers in 2019-2022.

sources.title: Insights on LTL Carrier Pickup and Delivery Operations
sources.supports: Carriers build routes for up to 20 or more stops a day; urban routes 50-60 miles, metro 90-100, peddle 150-200 or more; deliveries are unloaded first and pickups follow, and pickups relayed to the driver during the route cause backtracking; delivery appointments force re-sequencing; carriers track drive time, time at stop and delays; drivers moved from paper manifests to handhelds; key metrics stops per hour, miles per stop, shipments per stop; a 30-minute stop (driving plus time at stop) example; P&D absorbs 12-15% of shipment revenue.

sources.title: Terms and Conditions - Tariff 101 (16th revision, effective April 14, 2025)
sources.supports: Canadian domestic LTL rules under provincial conditions of carriage: regular pickup and delivery hours 6:00 AM to 6:00 PM; waiting-time free time on pickups and deliveries by billed weight (1-500 lb 15 min, 501-9,999 lb 30 min, 10,000-19,999 lb 1 h) then $25.25 per 15 min; attempted pickup charge $4.25/cwt, minimum $45; carrier provides only one employee (the driver) per vehicle and the consignor loads large or heavy articles; tailgate service up to 1,500 lb per lift; carrier liability $2.00/lb ($4.41/kg) unless higher value declared on the bill of lading; all shipments subject to re-weigh and measurement audit with a $25 rescale fee per pro; bill of lading changes must be authorised in writing; dangerous goods surcharge and excluded classes.

sources.title: Schedule a FedEx Freight pickup
sources.supports: General cutoff of 3 p.m. for automated pickup requests; online ready time no later than 3 p.m. local; same-day requests after 3 p.m. by phone to customer support or the local service centre; pickups booked same day or up to 10 business days ahead; request needs ready and close times at least 90 minutes apart, weight, number of handling units, package type and special services such as liftgate (no dock means a liftgate is needed); requests by web tool, phone or local service centre.

sources.title: TDG Bulletin: Shipping document
sources.supports: The consignor completes the shipping document before the carrier takes possession and a carrier may refuse an improperly documented shipment; road carriers keep a copy within the driver's reach; minimum content is UN number, shipping name, classes, packing group, quantity, number of labelled small containers, 24-hour number and consignor's certification; copies kept 2 years.

sources.title: TDG Bulletin: TDG Training
sources.supports: Anyone who handles, offers or transports dangerous goods must be adequately trained and hold an employer-issued training certificate (TDG Regulations s.6.1) or work under the direct physical supervision of a certified person; road certificates expire after 36 months.

sources.title: Summary of Maintenance and Safety Program Requirements for Alberta-Based Commercial Trucks / Tractors / Trailers
sources.supports: Daily trip inspection follows Schedule 1 of NSC Standard 13 Part 2; a trip inspection report records unit, odometer, carrier, location, each defect or no defect, date and time and the inspector's name and signature; a vehicle may not be driven with a major defect; reports kept 6 months; defects seen while driving must be recorded and reported; cargo must be contained, immobilised or secured so it cannot shift or fall (AR 121/2009 s.17(4), NSC Standard 10).

sources.title: Old Dominion Freight Line, Inc. Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2021
sources.supports: Service centres handle pickup and delivery in their local area; each night they load outbound freight for transport to other service centres; inbound freight arriving in the evening is generally scheduled for next-business-day delivery; LTL weight per shipment 1,571 lb (2021) and 1,614 lb (2020); 12,880 thousand LTL shipments in 2021; 23,663 employees including 11,802 drivers and 5,350 platform (dock) employees.

assumptions: The unit is one pickup stop; a stop carries about 1.5 shipments on average.

The daily trip inspection and the end-of-day check-in (timecard, defect reports) happen once per driver-day and are modelled in frt-ltl-pd-dispatch, which therefore produces the dvir and driver_timecard that the organisation file attaches to this process.

Paid time the driver spends waiting at the shipper (steps c, d, f, h) is counted as wait, not touch, so the labour cost per case excludes it; it averages roughly 15 to 20 minutes per pickup and should be added for full driver cost. Truck occupation on those steps does include it.

Trailer occupation on step t covers the hours the freight rides on the truck during the rest of the route; truck occupation counts only this pickup's share of driving so it is not double counted with other stops.
Shipper bill of lading is listed as a standing input rather than a trigger because the case starts from dispatch and the bill is handed over during the stop.

Staffing check: roles state 254 FTE; hands-on time of about 36 minutes per pickup times 100,000 pickups implies about 460 FTE at 130 productive hours a month. City drivers work about 9 to 10 paid hours a day (about 200 hours a month), so the implied headcount on 200 hours is about 300, near the stated 254. The organisation file's 540 city drivers look tight for 100,000 pickups plus the delivery stops.
